reference.source: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
clinicalPearls: A unilateral limitation of elevation of one eye in all horizontal positions, affecting the action of both elevators (superior rectus and inferior oblique), hence the older term double elevator palsy
Usually congenital: the affected eye is hypotropic in the primary position and the patient adopts a chin-up head posture to maintain binocular single vision
Ptosis or pseudoptosis is common; true ptosis occurs in roughly half of cases, and pseudoptosis from the hypotropic globe resolves when the eye elevates to fixate

Three mechanisms are recognised: restriction of the inferior rectus (positive forced duction, the commonest), primary elevator weakness (superior rectus and inferior oblique paresis), and a supranuclear cause
Forced duction and force generation testing differentiate a tight (restrictive) inferior rectus from a paretic cause and guide the choice of operation

If the patient fixates with the affected hypotropic eye, the sound eye shows a secondary hypertropia; a preserved Bell's phenomenon points to a supranuclear or paretic rather than restrictive mechanism
Marcus Gunn jaw-winking and other synkineses should be excluded when ptosis is present
Surgical choice depends on mechanism: inferior rectus recession for restriction and a Knapp procedure (transposition of the horizontal recti towards the superior rectus) for elevator weakness
reference.pathophysiology: Monocular elevation deficiency is a heterogeneous condition characterised by defective elevation of one eye. The commonest mechanism is a restrictive, tight inferior rectus (fibrosis) that mechanically prevents elevation; alternatively there may be a primary paresis of the elevator muscles (superior rectus and inferior oblique) or, less often, a supranuclear lesion of the elevation pathway in the pretectal region, in which case Bell's phenomenon is preserved. Many cases are congenital and may fall within the congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder spectrum. The resulting hypotropia in the primary position drives the compensatory chin-up head posture and, where the visual axes are not aligned, amblyopia of the affected eye.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles
Brown syndrome, which limits elevation only in adduction (key distinction)
Inferior rectus restriction from thyroid eye disease or an orbital floor fracture with entrapment
Superior oblique overaction and other causes of vertical strabismus
Skew deviation and supranuclear vertical gaze disturbance
Congenital ptosis with an apparent (pseudo) motility defect
additionalInvestigations: Forced duction testing for inferior rectus restriction and force generation testing
Orthoptic assessment across all positions of gaze with measurement of head posture
Assessment of Bell's phenomenon and saccadic velocities
Distinguishing true ptosis from pseudoptosis by rechecking lid height on fixation with the affected eye
Orbital CT or MRI if restriction from trauma, thyroid disease or a mass is suspected
Neuro-imaging if a supranuclear cause is suspected
redFlags: An acquired (rather than congenital) elevation deficit suggesting orbital, neurological or thyroid pathology
Signs of an orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment, including recent trauma and an oculocardiac reflex
Pupillary involvement or other neurological signs suggesting a third nerve or midbrain lesion
Amblyopia in a young child requiring prompt treatment
reference.prognosis: Congenital cases are non-progressive, and surgery to correct the hypotropia and abnormal head posture, combined with amblyopia treatment and ptosis repair where needed, generally gives good functional and cosmetic outcomes. Some limitation of elevation typically persists.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with Brown syndrome, which limits elevation only in adduction
Operating on ptosis before correcting the hypotropia, when pseudoptosis may resolve once the eye is realigned
Omitting forced ductions and thereby missing a restrictive inferior rectus, leading to the wrong operation
Overlooking amblyopia in the hypotropic eye
Assuming every case is paretic and missing a supranuclear cause by not checking Bell's phenomenon
